issues.title: (🐞) `Enum` with multiple values (`tuple`) can't be round tripped through json
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

```
pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for RootModel[A]
a
  Input should be (1, 2) [type=enum, input_value=[1, 2], input_type=list]
    For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.9/v/enum
```

`Enum`s support functionality where a tuple (["multiple values"](https://docs.python.org/3/library/enum.html#enum.Enum.__init__)) is assigned to the member

here, we see that pydantic does not support serialising and parsing of this type of `Enum` value

## Workaround

add a core schema to the class:
```py
    @classmethod
    def __get_pydantic_core_schema__(cls, source_type, handler):
        return core_schema.no_info_before_validator_function(
            lambda data: data if isinstance(data, cls) else tuple(data), handler(source_type)
        )
```

### Example Code

```Python
from enum import Enum

from pydantic import RootModel


class A(Enum):
    a = 1, 2


serialised = RootModel[A](A.a).model_dump_json()
parsed = RootModel[A].model_validate_json(serialised)
```

issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Overriding `__pyright_extra__` causes a `pyright` typing error because the type is not the same as the base declaration. 

### Example Code

```Python

ExtraDict = dict[str, int | str]

class ModelExtra(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="allow")
    __pydantic_extra__: ExtraDict = Field(init=False)


## Gives pyright error
#error: "__pydantic_extra__" overrides symbol of same name in class "BaseModel"
#    Variable is mutable so its type is invariant
#      Override type "ExtraDict" is not the same as base type "dict[str, Any] | None" (reportIncompatibleVariableOverride)

## BUT THIS ALSO BREAKS

class ModelExtra(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="allow")
    __pydantic_extra__: ExtraDict | None = Field(init=False)

## ERROR
```

comments.body:
I think the API to specify validation for extra fields is a bit flawed. While specifying it as an annotation is beneficial as you can then easily type check attribute accesses to `__pydantic_extra__`, there's a couple issues arising from this:
- type checkers treat `__pydantic_extra__` as a field, so using `=  Field(init=False)` is necessary as an ugly workaround
- if you set `extra` to `'allow'` without redefining `__pydantic_extra__` (because you don't want any specific validation to be applied), `__pydantic_extra__` is still annotated as `dict[str, Any] | None`, although at runtime it is guaranteed to _not_ be `None`
- you get the the pyright error because it is theorically unsafe to narrow the annotation, as `__pydantic_extra__` is considered mutable (see an explanation with a similar example [here](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/10699#issuecomment-2435517867)). In practice, I don't expect anyone to mutate the `__pydantic_extra__` dictionary directly. In fact, we provide a `model_extra` property to access the extra values. It is also flawed because the type of this property does not reflect the possibly overridden `__pydantic_extra__` annotation.

I can't come up with a good API immediately, however one thing that is certain is that we will have to break the existing API if we ever want to make changes here. As such, marking this issue as https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/labels/v3.

In the meanwhile, you can add a `pyright: ignore[reportIncompatibleVariableOverride]` comment or disable the error code at the project level (enabling this error code is debatable, see https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/issues/5933).

issues.title: Execution order of model validators with model inheritance
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Execution order of model validators in case of a `wrap` validator from a base class and an `after` validator from a subclass seems wrong, or at least the logic behind it eludes me :)

If you have defined a `wrap` model validator on a base class and an `after` model validator on a subclass, the `after` validator will be executed after the `wrap` validator has finished, i.e., the `after` validator of the subclass won't be "wrapped" by the `wrap` validator of the base class.

The output of the example code looks like this (when you comment out other validators):
```
BEGIN base_wrap_validator
END   base_wrap_validator
      sub_after_validator
```

I first thought that maybe all the validators of the base class are executed before proceeding with validators of the subclass, but when I added `before`/`after`/`wrap` validators on both the base class and the subclass, I got this:

```
BEGIN sub_wrap_validator
BEGIN base_wrap_validator
      sub_before_validator
      base_before_validator
      base_after_validator
END   base_wrap_validator
      sub_after_validator
END   sub_wrap_validator
```

So it seems that **the `before` validator of the subclass is indeed wrapped by the `wrap` validator of the base class, but the `after` validator is not**. This looks like a bug to me.

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel, model_validator


class Base(BaseModel):

    @model_validator(mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def base_before_validator(cls, v):
        print("      base_before_validator")
        return v

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def base_after_validator(self):
        print("      base_after_validator")
        return self

    @model_validator(mode="wrap")
    @classmethod
    def base_wrap_validator(cls, v, handler):
        print("BEGIN base_wrap_validator")
        v = handler(v)
        print("END   base_wrap_validator")
        return v


class Sub(Base):

    @model_validator(mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def sub_before_validator(cls, v):
        print("      sub_before_validator")
        return v

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def sub_after_validator(self):
        print("      sub_after_validator")
        return self

    @model_validator(mode="wrap")
    @classmethod
    def sub_wrap_validator(cls, v, handler):
        print("BEGIN sub_wrap_validator")
        v = handler(v)
        print("END   sub_wrap_validator")
        return v


sub = Sub()
```


### Python, Pydantic & OS Version


comments.body:
Hi, have scoured existing open and closed issues and have run into and read this [#8277](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/8277) already. Also read the existing documentation, including this section about ordering of validators within `Annotated`. However, still decided to create a new issue because:

-  I felt my use case wasn't covered by [#8277](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/8277) or any other issue I found. This [#8277](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/8277) shows a code example that is already covered by existing documentation, but maybe not clearly enough. I wouldn't be expecting a `before` validator to run before a `wrap` validator because [this section](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/validators/#before-after-wrap-and-plain-validators) of the documentation says the following:
> Wrap validators are the most flexible of all. You can run code **before or after Pydantic and other validators do their thing** or you can terminate validation immediately, both with a successful value or an error.

- I haven't found an existing issue that addresses validation order when you have model inheritance (this [#8277](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/8277) has everything in a single class). Model inheritance does introduce a new "dimension" because you can have a combination of validators of different types, some defined on the base class(es), some defined on the subclass(es). I would personally expect that Pydantic runs these validators in such a way that is equivalent to having a single class. If you have all three types of validators on a single class, the order of execution would be in line with the documentation (specifically, that paragraph I quoted in the previous point):
```
BEGIN base_wrap_validator
      base_before_validator
      base_after_validator
END   base_wrap_validator
```
If you compare this with the order of execution when you have a base class and a subclass, you can clearly see that the `sub_after_validator` is an "outlier".

- The documentation regarding ordering within `Annotated` seems clear to me, but this doesn't really apply to inheritance.


It all boils down to the question is this behavior (where an `after` subclass validator isn't being "wrapped" by a `wrap` base class validator) by design or is it a bug. If it's by design, for whatever reason, then, I guess, the only thing missing is documentation specifically saying that **the ordering of validators is different when you have a class hierarchy than when you have a single class**. If this [#8277](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/8277) represents the issue for this missing documentation, then my issue could indeed be marked as a duplicate of it :)

issues.title: Exporting models (recursively) without extra fields
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [X] I have read and followed [the docs](https://pydantic-docs.helpmanual.io) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

Previous discussion https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/discussions/3508

The `extra` model config offers great flexibility with options `ignore`, `allow`, or `forbid` that are used during model initialization. Also, there is the export option to specify fields to exclude from the returned dictionary using `exclude` parameter of `dict()` or `json()`.

**However, there is no option to recursively exclude extra fields while exporting a model.**

Example:

```py
class NestedModel(BaseModel):
    a: int = ...
    class Config:
        extra = Extra.allow

class Model(BaseModel):
    c: NestedModel = ...

model: Model = Model(c=NestedModel(a=20, b=22))

print(model.dict()) ## {'c': {'a': 20, 'b': 22}}
# how to exclude 'b' from the export without knowing the name of b upfront?
print()
```

### Suggested change: 
Add optional parameter `exclude_extra: bool = False` to `dict` and `json` which removes recursively all extra fields from the export when set to `True`.

Example:

```py
# Model from the previous snippet

print(model.dict(exclude_extra=True)) ## {'c': {'a': 20}}
```

Required code changes are [fairly simple](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/compare/main...mblo:pydantic:export-model-without-extra-fields). I'm aware of V2 plan, but wonder if this feature could be added.


### Affected Components

issues.title: `model_validate_json` confusing exception with union types (and divergence from `model_validate`)
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Given a union type between a `str` and an `Iterable[T]`, `model_load(json.loads(…))` and `model_load_json(…)` diverge in behavior, and, in particular, `model_load_json` can select the wrong arm of the union and raise an incorrect and confusing validation error.

See the example snippet below for a minimal reproducer.

(If you're wondering **why** I am trying to work with such a type, it appears in [Anthropic's SDK](https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python/blob/3ad63dbcded3b9d3a20319ec8155473cb4c137d2/src/anthropic/types/tool_result_block_param.py#L16-L23))


### Example Code

```Python
import json
from typing import Iterable

from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing_extensions import Required, TypedDict


class Inner(TypedDict):
    msg: Required[str]


class Outer(BaseModel):
    content: str | Iterable[Inner]


def force(x):
    """Force validation if x is a lazy ValidationIterator"""
    if isinstance(x, str):
        return x
    return list(x)


model = Outer(content="Hello")

json_text = model.model_dump_json()
print(f"JSON: {json_text}")

# model_validate(json.loads(...)) works fine
obj = Outer.model_validate(json.loads(json_text))
obj.content = force(obj.content)
print("model_validate(json.loads):", obj)

# But this will try to validate `"Hello"` against the
# `Iterable[Inner]`, and fail!
obj = Outer.model_validate_json(json_text)
obj.content = force(obj.content)
print("model_validate_json:", obj)
```

issues.title: `discriminator` can be silently misused
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Users can apply `discriminator='tag'` to the individual union elements and it's silently ignored. We should warn on this case as validation may be unexpectedly wrong.

Noticed at https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/1449#issuecomment-2370842447

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, TypeAdapter
from typing import Annotated, Literal

class A1(BaseModel):
    tag: Literal["A"]

    def __repr__(self):
        return "A1()"

class A2(BaseModel):
    tag: Literal["A"]

    def __repr__(self):
        return "A2()"
    

Wrong = Annotated[A1, Field(..., discriminator='tag')] | Annotated[A2, Field(..., discriminator='tag')]

# Should have been:
# A = Annotated[A1 | A2, Field(..., discriminator='tag')]

TypeAdapter(Wrong).validate_python({'tag': 'A'})
```

```Text
2.9.2
```

issues.title: Fields marked as `Final` with a default value shouldn't be considered as class variables
issues.body:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Currently:

```python
from typing import Final

from pydantic import BaseModel

class Model(BaseModel):
    a: Final[int]
    b: Final[int] = 1

Model.model_fields.keys()
#> dict_keys(['a'])
Model.__class_vars__
#> {'b'}
```

Instead, we should follow [the typing specification update from this year](https://github.com/python/typing/pull/1669), i.e. final fields with a default value are still considered as fields, and not as class variables. I'll also note that the behavior is broken when using `Annotated` (i.e. using `Annotated[Final[int], ...] = 1` is not considered a class variable).

TODO:
- [x] Add a deprecation/user warning when a final field with a default value is used. The warning should tell the user to explicitly use `ClassVar`.
  - https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/11168 
- [ ] In V3, change the behavior, and update the mypy plugin as necessary. There's also a TODO in `FieldInfo.from_annotated_attribute()`: if the `Final` qualifier is used as is (without an explicit type), we should try our best to infer the type from the default (if any). If the assignment is _not_ a `FieldInfo` instance, it is the default value and we can simply do `type(assignment)`. Else, if the final `FieldInfo` instance has a `default`, apply the same. If it has a `default_factory`, we should try our best but let's not complicate things to much: if the default factory is a type (e.g. `dict`, `list`, that when called results in an "empty" instance), use it as the type. Else, infer the type as `Any`.

crossref https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/10474#issuecomment-2478666651, https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/2768#issuecomment-2027592572, https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/9904.

comments.body:
I reproduced this on the latest release (2.13.4) and ran a few extra checks that might help pin it down.

Two small notes first:

1. The snippet in the issue description needs `from __future__ import annotations` (or a quoted forward ref) — as written, `child: NodeVal | None = None` raises `NameError: name 'NodeVal' is not defined` at class definition.
2. The reporter's guess ("presumably due to prebuilt validators logic") doesn't fit: I tested `PYDANTIC_PREBUILT_VALIDATORS=0` with no effect, and the double-call also reproduces on **2.11.10** — prebuilt validators only became the default in 2.12.

## Verified diagnostics (2.13.4)

| Case | Calls |
|---|---|
| Top-level `NodeVal.model_validate({})` | 1 |
| As a field: `OuterVal.model_validate({'node': {}})` | **2** |
| Two-level tree (`{'node': {'child': {}}}`) | **3** (2 for the outer instance + 1 for the child) |
| `mode='before'` variant (same recursive model) | 1 |
| Non-recursive control (same shape, no self-reference) | 1 |

So the double-call is specific to `model_validator(mode='after')` **on the recursive path**: the instance that is validated as a field of another model runs its after-validator twice, while the same model validated at top level runs it once.

## Regression boundary

Tested across releases:

| Version | Calls |
|---|---|
| 2.9.2 | 1 |
| 2.10.0 / 2.10.6 | 1 |
| **2.11.0** and later | **2** |

The bug was introduced in **2.11.0** (which shipped a schema-building rework for lower memory usage) — not in 2.12's prebuilt validators.

I'd like to work on this: a focused regression test on the recursive `after`-validator path (asserting single invocation), plus the fix if it lands in pydantic-core. Could you assign it to me?

comments.body:
I've confirmed this on current `main` (`f59e929c9`) with mypy 1.18.2:

```python
from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, RootModel

class A(BaseModel):
    name: Literal['a']

class B(RootModel[str]):
    pass

a = A(name='a')
b = B('a')

a == 'a'  # flagged: Non-overlapping equality check (correct)
b == 'a'  # NOT flagged, but should be — same inconsistency reported here
```

Root cause: `BaseModel.__eq__` (`pydantic/main.py`) is defined inside `if not TYPE_CHECKING:`, so mypy never sees it and falls back to `object`'s default overlap semantics — which is what lets `--strict-equality` correctly flag `a == 'a'`. `RootModel.__eq__` (`pydantic/root_model.py:149`) is defined **outside** any `TYPE_CHECKING` guard, with a fully-visible `other: Any` signature, so mypy sees an `Any`-typed method and never flags anything.

`RootModel.__eq__` has real runtime behavior (it compares `root` field annotations before delegating to `super().__eq__()`), so it can't just move into a `TYPE_CHECKING` stub — it needs to follow the same `if not TYPE_CHECKING:` pattern `BaseModel.__eq__` already uses, so mypy stops seeing the `Any`-typed signature while the method still executes normally at runtime.

Happy to send a PR for this (single file, mirrors an existing pattern, plus mypy test fixtures under `tests/mypy/`) — could I get this assigned to me?

Potential fix is in `__eq__` from BaseModel, avoiding using direct `__dict__` comparison and sanitize first for self referencing:

```py
class A(BaseModel):
```

```python

│   'type': 'model',
│   'cls': <class '__main__.PreferredCurrencies'>,
│   'schema': {
│   │   'type': 'model-fields',
│   │   'fields': {
│   │   │   'currency_one': {
│   │   │   │   'type': 'model-field',
│   │   │   │   'schema': {
│   │   │   │   │   'function': {'type': 'no-info', 'function': operator.attrgetter('value')},
│   │   │   │   │   'schema': {'type': 'definition-ref', 'schema_ref': '__main__.Currency:94912979623376'},  # <-- inlined
│   │   │   │   │   'serialization': {'type': 'function-plain', 'function': <function GenerateSchema._enum_schema.<locals>.<lambda> at 0x79ca5910e2a0>},
│   │   │   │   │   'type': 'function-after'
│   │   │   │   },
│   │   │   │   'metadata': {}
│   │   │   },
│   │   │   'currency_two': {
│   │   │   │   'type': 'model-field',
│   │   │   │   'schema': {
│   │   │   │   │   'function': {'type': 'no-info', 'function': operator.attrgetter('value')},
│   │   │   │   │   'schema': {'type': 'definition-ref', 'schema_ref': '__main__.Currency:94912979623376'},  # <-- inlined
│   │   │   │   │   'serialization': {'type': 'function-plain', 'function': <function GenerateSchema._enum_schema.<locals>.<lambda> at 0x79ca5910e3e0>},
│   │   │   │   │   'type': 'function-after'
│   │   │   │   },
│   │   │   │   'metadata': {}
│   │   │   }
│   │   },
│   │   'model_name': 'PreferredCurrencies',
│   │   'computed_fields': []
│   }
}
```

The schema for the `__main__.Currency:94912979623376` enum is:

```python
{
│   'type': 'enum',
│   'cls': <enum 'Currency'>,
│   'members': [<Currency.USD: 'USD'>, <Currency.CAD: 'CAD'>],
│   'ref': '__main__.Currency:94912979623376',
│   'metadata': {'<stripped>'}
}
```
and as we can see, it was inlined for both fields. Note that the core schema for the two fields are of type `function-after`. It's basically an after validator that will do `getattr(enum_value, 'value')`, essentially converting `Currency.USD/CAD` to `'USD'/'CAD'`. This is only done if `use_enum_values` is used. 

- We generate the core schema for `TestModel2`. We enter the core schema generation for field `TestModel2.preferred_currencies`. because it refers to `PreferredCurrencies`, we use the cached `__pydantic_core_schema__` property from it. `_generate_schema_from_property` has the effect of calling `_unpack_refs_defs`:
https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/blob/fba836a616d301b8dadf48d404bb4791642f1bf5/pydantic/_internal/_generate_schema.py#L717-L726

Meaning the definition for the `Currency` enum from the previous code block will be added to the definitions of the current `GenerateSchema` class (and notice that it is the schema without the after validator!).

- We enter the core schema generation for field `TestModel2.currency`. Because the definition of the `Currency` enum is already in the saved defs, it is reused as is.

---

So at first glance, looks like the `ref` of the enum schema is not put at the right place. Instead (if `use_enum_values` is used), it should be put on the after validator schema. **However**, what happens if the `PreferredCurrencies` did not have `use_enum_values` set, but `TestModel2` did? Haven't tested, but I believe we will end up with the same issue. Perhaps a different reference should be generated, depending on the `use_enum_values` (not ideal)? Could https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/issues/1337 solve the issue?

issues.title: Next steps for `Url` like types
issues.body:
In https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/10766 and https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/10662, we made the switch for url like types to be proper Python classes, which helps to clean up behavior in terms of `isinstance` checks and type checking for various constraints (ex - if `host_required` is `True` for a given url type, `host` is typed as `str` rather than `str | None`).

There's still more to be done to clean up this implementation, and more to be done on the URL front in general. The long term goal is to have url structures sort of mimic the proposal outlined here: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/10032.

One unique thing about url types is that we validate on `__init__`, sort of like we do for `BaseModel` or `pydantic_dataclass` types.

There are a few specific improvements that I think we could make in the short term:
* We could use a `SchemaValidator` instead of a `TypeAdapter` internally, which might simplify "schema build" time for said types.
* We should simplify the `PyUrl` and `PyMultiHost` url types if possible, as they're no longer meant to be public - perhaps a more simple struct could work well?
* It feels like we could simplify `__init__` to make validation more performant - need to look into this.
* Admittedly, it's not super performant to have a wrap validator involved here - can we get away from this while still supporting these types in Python?

One idea we tossed around for a bit was adding a `cls` attribute to the `url_schema` construct in `pydantic-core`, so we could construct the appropriate type there. However, this doesn't make a lot of sense, given that we're currently just storing a `_url` attribute on the more constrained url classes. So, if we were to move to this `cls` construction approach, I don't think the more `RustModel` like approach would make sense here.

There are many change requests and issues associated with urls that parallel this issue, a few of which are seen here:
* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/7186
* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/8244
* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/9794
* https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/8061

### Initial Checks

### Description

I'm using Pydantic with Django models (and FastAPI). I have a use case where I have a DJango model that has a couple of GenericForeignKeys to other models, and I'm using Discriminated Unions to detect the correct schema to use when serializing these objects. 

With Pydantic `2.8.2`, this works perfectly, but after updating to `2.9.1` things broke down. What happens is that the union field's value is returned as a string, almost as if `repr()` was called on it. Maybe there's an internal serializer that's called twice?

I re-read the documentation about the feature, and at a quick glance didn't spot any functionality changes. I also checked the changelog, and one of these PRs might have introduced something causing this:
https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/1397
https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/1398

I've tested `2.9.0` and its beta versions through to the just released `2.9.2`. `2.8.2` is the last version where this works.

### Example Code

```Python
import typing as t

import pydantic
from django.contrib.contenttypes.fields import GenericForeignKey
from django.contrib.contenttypes.models import ContentType
from django.db import models


class GenericModel(models.Model):
    target_content_type = models.ForeignKey(ContentType, ...)
    target_object_id = models.IntegerField()
    target = GenericForeignKey(ct_field='target_content_type', fk_field='target_object_id')


class FirstTarget(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=255)


class SecondTarget(models.Model):
    something = models.IntegerField()


ModelSchemaMapping = dict[
    t.Type[models.Model],
    t.Type[pydantic.BaseModel]
]


def get_generic_fk_schema(mapping: ModelSchemaMapping):
    fallback_tag = 'Other'

    def discriminator_func(v):
        if isinstance(v, tuple(mapping.keys())):
            # This returns the Django model name, like 'FirstTarget'
            return v._meta.object_name
        return fallback_tag

    valid_choices = [
        t.Annotated[
            schema,
            pydantic.Tag(model._meta.object_name)
        ]
        for model, schema in mapping.items()
    ]

    return t.Annotated[
        t.Union[
            *valid_choices,
            # Fallback that only returns the model's primary key as the union value.
            # Basically this shouldn't happen if I've defined my mappings correctly.
            t.Annotated[
                int,
                pydantic.BeforeValidator(lambda obj: obj.pk),
                pydantic.Tag(fallback_tag)
            ]
        ],
        pydantic.Discriminator(discriminator_func)
    ]


class DjangoSchema(pydantic.BaseModel):
    model_config = pydantic.ConfigDict(
        from_attributes=True,
        arbitrary_types_allowed=True
    )


class FirstSchema(DjangoSchema):
    id: int
    name: str


class SecondSchema(DjangoSchema):
    id: int
    something: int


class GenericSchema(DjangoSchema):
    id: int
    target: get_generic_fk_schema({
        FirstTarget: FirstSchema,
        SecondTarget: SecondSchema
    })


first_obj = FirstTarget.objects.create(name='foobar')
generic_obj = GenericModel.objects.create(
    target_content_type=ContentType.objects.get_for_model(FirstTarget),
    target_object_id=first_obj.pk
)

schema = GenericSchema(target=generic_obj.target)  # target == first_obj
schema.model_dump()

# Expected result
{'id': 1, 'target': {'id': 1, 'name': 'foobar'}}

# Actual result
```

### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

## Update:

Please see the comment here for the current status of this issue: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/10654#issuecomment-2423475533

tl;dr:
the bug:  one needs to manually define `__pydantic_serializer__` on custom classes in addition to specifying a serialization schema in `__get_pydantic_core_schema__` when they are used as a type in `__pydantic_extra__`. 

the nice-to-have: The serialization warnings are cryptic and make it hard to diagnose when you have provided an invalid serialization schema :( (related to https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/10495 )

---

### Description

I have an edge case that i swear is an actual problem and not just esoteric bughunting.

To support multiple array backends from a single `NDArray` type in [numpydantic](https://github.com/p2p-ld/numpydantic), I use it as an abstract passthrough class that validates the data but then returns one of potentially multiple types (numpy ndarray, dask array, proxy to an hdf5 array, etc., more info in [docs](https://numpydantic.readthedocs.io/en/latest/interfaces.html)).

This works, including roundtrip json serialization, *except* when the type is specified on the `__pydantic_extra__` field like `__pydantic_extra__: dict[str, NDArray]` . Then pydantic seems to lose the connection between the object that's passed through and the `NDArray` object, and attempts to serialize the object directly (rather than using the serialization schema created by `NDArray.__get_pydantic_core_schema__` ). 

I have been trying to work around this by giving `__pydantic_serializer__` declarations to the passed through types, but i have been running up against a consistent problem with the recursion checker:

```
pydantic_core._pydantic_core.PydanticSerializationError: Error serializing to JSON: ValueError: Circular reference detected (id repeated)
```

I've dug around in that code a bit, and it seems like it's a very tight check whether or not an id has been seen before, but I can't really tell here where it might have been repeated. I'm not sure what a fix here looks like because i can't tell if this is a bug or i'm doing something wrong. 

I fully acknowledge this is a relatively offroad, nonstandard usages of maybe not fully finished APIs, so apologize in advance.  If it does look like a bug to y'all, i would be happy to help with a patch, as i am always looking for more reasons to learn more about bilingual rust/python projects <3.

Below is a MWE that reproduces the error so you don't have to dig through all the numpydantic code :)

edit1: More info - i can't set a python debugger in the serialization function, so i assume (?) this happens before we actually reach it and try and call it

edit2: it appears as if it's not limited to `extra` fields, and it happens for any passthrough class like this, MWE updated to show that and the other pair of cases for when the serialization function is defined on the validating class and why it is necessary to declare the serialization function on the passed through class in the first place

### Example Code

When the serializer is on the passed-through class:

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict
from pydantic_core import SchemaSerializer, core_schema


def jsonize(x):
    return [1,2,3]

def passthrough(x):
    return x

class SerializableClass:

    __pydantic_serializer__ = SchemaSerializer(
        core_schema.plain_serializer_function_ser_schema(
            jsonize, when_used="json"
        )
    )
    
class AnnotationClass:
    
    def __get_pydantic_core_schema__(self, *args):
        return core_schema.no_info_plain_validator_function(
            passthrough
        )


class MyModel(BaseModel):
    real_field: AnnotationClass | None = None
    __pydantic_extra__: dict[str, AnnotationClass]

    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="allow")

# Fails - Circular reference
instance = MyModel(real_field=SerializableClass())
instance.model_dump_json()

# Fails - Circular Reference
instance = MyModel(extra_field=SerializableClass())
instance.model_dump_json()
```

When the serializer is on the validation class:

```python

        return core_schema.no_info_plain_validator_function(
            passthrough,
            serialization=core_schema.plain_serializer_function_ser_schema(
                jsonize, when_used="json"
            )
        )
```

So we correctly arrive at the infer serialization method, here: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/blob/92a259ea10113e0d41dea5b14dc8745e3bf671ef/src/serializers/infer.rs#L356

Then we make a recursion guard, which triggers inserting the id of the `value` into the `extra`'s recursion state, and also causes the first print of the traceback: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/blob/92a259ea10113e0d41dea5b14dc8745e3bf671ef/src/serializers/infer.rs#L365

Then we continue and also correctly match against `ObType::PydanticSerializable`, and that seems to start the serialization process over again, where now through the `AnySerializer` we repeat the same infer loop and land back at `serializers/infer.rs#L365`, instantiating the recursion guard again with the same object twice.

So this leads me to suspect that the passthrough part is irrelevant, and in fact any object that has a `__pydantic_serializer__` in `__pydantic_extra__` will fail.

I confirmed this with this MWE

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict
from pydantic_core import SchemaSerializer, core_schema

def jsonize(x):
    return [1,2,3]

class SerializableClass:

    __pydantic_serializer__ = SchemaSerializer(
        core_schema.plain_serializer_function_ser_schema(
            jsonize, when_used="json"
        )
    )

    @classmethod
    def __get_pydantic_core_schema__(self, *args):
        return core_schema.any_schema()
    

class MyModel(BaseModel):
    real_field: SerializableClass | None = None
    __pydantic_extra__: dict[str, SerializableClass]

    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="allow")

# Fails - Circular reference
instance = MyModel(real_field=SerializableClass())
instance.model_dump_json()

# Fails - Circular Reference
instance = MyModel(extra_field=SerializableClass())
instance.model_dump_json()
```

Interestingly, that also fails when instantiating the model without having any actual extra field (the `real_field` case above) - it seems as if having an annotation like `__pydantic_extra__: dict[str, SerializableClass]` is enough to trigger the behavior, which is somewhat surprising to me, because my expectation would be that if i didn't pass any extra values that that annotation would be unused (i.e., being an "extra" field, i would expect the value in the dict to always implicitly be `Optional[T]`).

As in the initial set of examples, if i instead declare the serializer function in `__get_pydantic_core_schema__`, i am back to getting "`Unable to serialize unknown type: <SerializableClass>`" on the second case where it is supplied as `extra_field` despite `SerializableClass` having a pydantic core schema.

```python
class SerializableClass:

    def __get_pydantic_core_schema__(self, *args):
        return core_schema.any_schema(serialization=core_schema.plain_serializer_function_ser_schema(
            jsonize, when_used="json"
        ))
```
